note: English- and French-held areas, siege camps and campaign routes are approximate reconstructions traced from period maps (Johnston's historical atlas, Commons campaign maps) and dated from cited statements; there were no continuous front lines, so control is shown as held areas and campaigns as arrows.

baseYears.why: the border data's own outlines for 1415–1453 put Brittany, the Pays de Caux and a fixed Normandy under England and miss the Loire towns; the 1414 borders (England: Gascony and Calais) are shown and English-held France is drawn as occupation areas

chapters.title: Crécy and Calais
arrows: Edward III's march from La Hougue to Crécy and Calais
Philip VI follows Edward from Paris to Crécy
chapters.text: Edward III landed in the Cotentin on 12 July 1346 and marched across Normandy, sacking Caen, burning his way along the Seine to within sight of Paris and slipping over the Somme at Blanchetaque. At Crécy on 26 August his longbowmen and dismounted men-at-arms destroyed the charges of Philip VI's much larger army. Edward then besieged Calais, which surrendered on 3 August 1347 and stayed English for two centuries.

chapters.title: The Black Prince's raids and Poitiers
arrows: The Black Prince's chevauchée to Narbonne
The Black Prince's raid from Bergerac to the Loire and Poitiers
John II crosses the Loire at Blois to cut off the Black Prince
chapters.text: From English Gascony, Edward the Black Prince led a great mounted raid in autumn 1355 to Narbonne near the Mediterranean and back, burning towns but taking no land. In August 1356 he struck north towards the Loire; King John II crossed the river at Blois to cut him off. At Poitiers on 19 September the outnumbered Anglo-Gascons won and captured the French king himself.

chapters.title: The Reims campaign and the Treaty of Brétigny
arrows: Edward III marches from Calais to Reims
Edward III's march through Burgundy to Paris and Chartres
chapters.text: Edward III landed at Calais in October 1359 hoping to be crowned at Reims, but the city held out and he lifted the siege in January. He marched through Burgundy to Paris and on towards Chartres, where a hailstorm battered his army. By the Treaty of Brétigny (May 1360, ratified at Calais in October) Edward gave up his claim to the French crown in return for a greatly enlarged Aquitaine, Calais and Ponthieu in full sovereignty.

chapters.title: Charles V wins it back
arrows: Du Guesclin's reconquest of Poitou
John of Gaunt's great chevauchée from Calais to Bordeaux
chapters.text: War resumed in 1369. Charles V and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin avoided pitched battles and retook the Brétigny lands town by town; a Castilian fleet destroyed an English convoy off La Rochelle in June 1372 and Poitiers and La Rochelle fell soon after. John of Gaunt's great raid from Calais to Bordeaux in 1373 achieved little, and by 1374 England held only Calais and the coastal strip of Gascony.

chapters.title: Harfleur and Agincourt
arrows: Henry V lands at Chef-de-Caux and besieges Harfleur
Henry V's march from Harfleur by way of Agincourt to Calais
chapters.text: Henry V reopened the war in August 1415 by besieging Harfleur at the mouth of the Seine, which surrendered on 22 September after his army had been ravaged by dysentery. Marching for Calais, he found the Somme crossings held and had to go far upstream. On 25 October at Agincourt his small, exhausted army destroyed a much larger French force in the mud, and four days later he reached Calais.

chapters.title: The conquest of Normandy
arrows: Henry V lands at Touques and takes Caen
English sweep through Lower Normandy to Alençon
Gloucester clears the Cotentin to Cherbourg
Henry V advances on Rouen and besieges it
Henry V pushes up the Seine to Pontoise
chapters.text: Henry V came back in August 1417 to conquer, not raid. He took Caen in September and Falaise over the winter, and his brothers cleared Lower Normandy and the Cotentin. Rouen, starved by a six-month siege, surrendered on 19 January 1419, and the fall of Pontoise at the end of July opened the road to Paris. Only Mont-Saint-Michel held out for France.

chapters.title: The Treaty of Troyes: English France at its height
arrows: Henry V and Burgundy take Sens, Montereau and Melun
Bedford completes the conquest of Maine
chapters.text: The murder of Duke John the Fearless in September 1419 drove Burgundy, which already held Paris, into alliance with England. By the Treaty of Troyes (May 1420) Henry V became heir to the French throne, and English and Burgundian troops ruled northern France while the Dauphin Charles held the south from Bourges. A French and Scottish army won at Baugé in 1421, but the English triumphed at Verneuil in 1424, and by 1428 their rule stretched from the Channel to the Loire.

chapters.title: Joan of Arc: Orléans and Reims
arrows: Salisbury's army takes the Loire towns and besieges Orléans
Joan of Arc's relief army reaches Orléans
Loire campaign: Jargeau, Meung, Beaugency and Patay
Charles VII's coronation march from Gien to Reims
Charles VII's army turns towards Paris
chapters.text: The English besieged Orléans from October 1428, ringing it with forts. Joan of Arc arrived with a relief force at the end of April 1429, and on 8 May the English abandoned the siege. In June the French retook the Loire towns and routed the English at Patay; Charles VII then marched through Burgundian-held Champagne, whose towns opened their gates, and was crowned at Reims in July. An assault on Paris failed on 8 September.

chapters.title: Burgundy changes sides and Paris is lost
arrows: Rising in the Pays de Caux: Dieppe to Harfleur
Richemont and Dunois retake Paris
chapters.text: At the Congress of Arras in September 1435 Philip of Burgundy made peace with Charles VII, leaving the English alone. Before the year was out the French, helped by a peasant rising, had taken Dieppe, Harfleur and the rest of the Pays de Caux. On 13 April 1436 the citizens of Paris let Richemont's army in, and four days later the English garrison left for Rouen.

chapters.title: The French reconquest of Normandy
arrows: Dunois's army takes the Seine towns and Rouen
Kyriell's relief army marches from Cherbourg towards Caen
Clermont's army closes in at Formigny
The French take Bayeux and besiege Caen
The French close on Cherbourg
chapters.text: When the truce broke down in 1449, Charles VII's reorganised army, with a strong artillery train, swept into Normandy: Rouen fell in October, Harfleur in December and Honfleur in January 1450. An English relief army that landed at Cherbourg was destroyed at Formigny on 15 April. Caen surrendered on 1 July, Falaise on 21 July and Cherbourg, the last English stronghold in Normandy, on 12 August 1450.

chapters.title: Gascony lost: Castillon
arrows: Dunois conquers the Bordelais
The French march on Bayonne
Talbot lands near Bordeaux and retakes the city
Talbot marches to relieve Castillon
Charles VII's armies converge on Castillon
The French take Libourne and besiege Bordeaux
chapters.text: The French turned to Gascony, English for three centuries: Bordeaux surrendered on 30 June 1451 and Bayonne on 20 August. The Gascons called the English back, and John Talbot retook Bordeaux in October 1452. On 17 July 1453 Talbot attacked the French artillery camp at Castillon and was killed with much of his army. Bordeaux gave up on 19 October, leaving England only Calais.

battles.name: Battle of Caen
battles.casualties: c. 5,000 French soldiers and civilians killed; English losses light

battles.name: Battle of Crécy
battles.casualties: French: c. 1,500–4,000 men-at-arms killed and heavy infantry losses; English: 100–300 killed

battles.name: Battle of Poitiers
battles.casualties: French: over 4,500 men-at-arms killed or captured and 1,500–3,800 infantry; Anglo-Gascon losses much lighter

battles.name: Battle of Pontvallain
battles.casualties: most of an English army of 4,000–6,000 killed or captured; French losses light

battles.name: Battle of La Rochelle (naval)
battles.casualties: the English fleet destroyed or captured, with hundreds killed and the Earl of Pembroke taken prisoner

battles.name: Siege of Harfleur
battles.casualties: English: c. 2,000 dead, mostly of dysentery, and as many sent home sick; garrison losses small

battles.name: Battle of Agincourt
battles.casualties: French: c. 6,000 killed and 700–2,200 captured; English: up to 600 killed

battles.name: Siege of Rouen
battles.casualties: c. 12,000 civilians died, many of hunger; troop losses unknown

battles.name: Battle of Baugé
battles.casualties: English: c. 1,000 killed and 500 captured; Franco-Scottish losses very light

battles.name: Siege of Meaux
battles.casualties: English: more than 6,000 men lost, largely to disease

battles.name: Battle of Verneuil
battles.casualties: Franco-Scottish: c. 6,000 killed and 200 captured; English: c. 1,600 killed

battles.name: Battle of Patay
battles.casualties: English: 2,000–4,000 killed or captured; French losses very light

battles.name: Battle of Formigny
battles.casualties: English: most of an army of c. 4,000 killed or captured; French: 500–1,000 killed or wounded

battles.name: Battle of Castillon
battles.casualties: English: c. 4,000 killed or captured, Talbot among the dead; French: c. 100
